Title: Use hidden YAML + compiled AST for workflow definitions
Context: We need readable, versionable workflow definitions but safe execution.
Decision: AI generates a typed AST; system validates; YAML is rendered for storage/export/advanced view; runtime executes AST, not raw Markdown.
Consequences: Combines GitHub Actions-like readability with schema safety.
Alternatives: Raw JSON only; Markdown skills only; visual nodes only.

Title: Use Inngest as durable orchestrator
Context: Workflows need retries, waits, approval pauses, events, monitoring, and cancellation.
Decision: Use Inngest for durable step orchestration while keeping our own workflow interpreter.
Consequences: Avoids building low-level workflow infra from scratch.
Alternatives: Vercel Workflows; Temporal; custom queue.

Title: Use Next.js + Vercel deployment
Context: Solo/bootstrapped developer needs fast full-stack deployment and Vercel Sandbox compatibility.
Decision: Use Next.js App Router hosted on Vercel.
Consequences: Fast iteration and tight sandbox/deployment integration.
Alternatives: AWS-only; custom Node server; Remix.

Title: Use Postgres + Drizzle ORM
Context: Need relational consistency, JSONB AST storage, versioning, audit logs.
Decision: Use Postgres with Drizzle migrations and typed schema.
Consequences: Good balance of typing, SQL, JSONB, and speed.
Alternatives: Prisma; Supabase-only client; MongoDB.

Title: Use better-auth for auth and organizations
Context: Need modern auth with org/team extension path.
Decision: Use better-auth, extend with org/membership tables if needed.
Consequences: Avoids building auth from scratch.
Alternatives: NextAuth/Auth.js; Clerk; Supabase Auth.

Title: Use Vercel Sandbox for code/file execution
Context: AI needs to create/run scripts safely without touching production server.
Decision: Execute generated .py/.js/.sh only in Vercel Sandbox.
Consequences: Keeps code execution isolated and compatible with Vercel stack.
Alternatives: E2B; Modal; Daytona; local Docker.

Title: Use Composio plus direct APIs for tools
Context: Need broad app access but also control for critical tools.
Decision: Use Composio for breadth; implement direct APIs for high-value integrations if needed.
Consequences: Accelerates connector coverage while preserving platform-level policy.
Alternatives: Build all connectors; only MCP; only direct APIs.

Title: Approval required for external actions
Context: Trust is core; autonomous send/post/update can cause harm.
Decision: All send/post/publish/update external actions require approval by default.
Consequences: Reduces risk and improves user trust.
Alternatives: Allow auto actions from day one.

Title: Append-only event log as execution truth
Context: Need debuggability, replay, timeline, audit, pulse feed.
Decision: Every run emits events into workflow_events and optional events.jsonl.
Consequences: Enables live timeline and support debugging.
Alternatives: Only store final statuses.

Title: Use SSE for live run updates first
Context: Run events are one-way from server to client; SSE is simpler than WebSockets.
Decision: Use SSE endpoint per run; polling fallback.
Consequences: Lower complexity and sufficient for MVP.
Alternatives: WebSockets; hosted realtime; polling only.

Title: Simple UX first, Advanced YAML second
Context: Users should not face YAML unless they choose advanced mode.
Decision: Prompt, preview, cards, approvals, artifacts are primary UI.
Consequences: Avoids n8n/Beam complexity.
Alternatives: YAML editor first; node canvas first.

Title: Use model router with cheap/strong roles
Context: Costs must be controlled for bootstrap economics.
Decision: Route compiler/hard reasoning to stronger model; routine tasks to cheap model; scripts for deterministic work.
Consequences: Cheaper than broad single-agent execution.
Alternatives: One expensive model for all tasks.

Title: Use safe YAML subset
Context: YAML can contain unsafe/custom constructs and ambiguity.
Decision: Parse restricted YAML, reject custom tags/unknown keys, validate schema.
Consequences: Prevents unsafe execution and weird parser behavior.
Alternatives: Trust arbitrary YAML.

Title: Use workflow credits for billing
Context: Autonomous workflows have variable model/tool/sandbox costs.
Decision: Meter usage events and charge workflow credits with hard caps.
Consequences: Prevents free/low-tier abuse and surprise costs.
Alternatives: Flat unlimited $20 plan.

Title: No public workflow marketplace in MVP
Context: Public arbitrary workflows/scripts create security risk.
Decision: Start with private workflows and curated internal templates only.
Consequences: Reduces supply-chain and abuse risk.
Alternatives: Open public marketplace immediately.

Title: Use templates as starting points, not product core
Context: Templates help onboarding, but core is prompt-to-workflow compiler.
Decision: Library contains premade workflows; users can prompt from scratch.
Consequences: Balances simplicity and capability.
Alternatives: Template-only product.

Title: Use tool router instead of exposing all tools
Context: All-tool context is expensive and risky.
Decision: Expose only relevant tool schemas per step after permission filtering.
Consequences: Reduces token cost and wrong tool calls.
Alternatives: Dump all tools into model context.

Title: Build three proof workflows for MVP
Context: Need prove engine with concrete value without overbuilding.
Decision: Social content, inbox drafts, lead research.
Consequences: Covers research, files, tools, approvals, schedules, memory.
Alternatives: Attempt universal workflows on day one.

Title: Remove checked-in E2B template payload from active base
Context: The repo is moving to Vercel Sandbox behind a provider-neutral interface, while checked-in E2B desktop templates preserve old Manus assumptions.
Decision: Delete checked-in E2B templates and local-template scripts; keep E2B runtime code only as temporary compatibility.
Consequences: Reduces repo noise and prevents the old E2B desktop image from becoming the new foundation.
Alternatives: Keep templates; rename them as Vercel templates; delete all E2B code immediately.

Title: Defer non-cleanup type debt to upgrade phase
Context: Cleanup verification exposed AI SDK/Zod/orchestrator type drift that is not caused by deleted files and will move again during package upgrades.
Decision: Do not chase non-cleanup type debt during deletion-first cleanup; document it and fix it during package-family upgrades.
Consequences: Keeps cleanup focused and avoids stabilizing old APIs before reset.
Alternatives: Fix all type errors now; ignore verification; upgrade packages during cleanup.

Title: Use DB-backed trigger registry
Context: User workflows can define many schedules and event triggers; creating one cron/route/function per trigger would not scale.
Decision: Store user-defined triggers in workflow_triggers and use static scheduler/event-router functions to emit workflow/run.requested.
Consequences: Dynamic triggers become auditable product data with rate limits, dedupe, jitter, misfire policy, and plan controls.
Alternatives: One Vercel Cron per trigger; one Inngest function per workflow; external scheduler SaaS per trigger.

Title: Use static Inngest functions for runtime execution
Context: Runtime needs durable waits, retries, approvals, callbacks, event routing, and observability while workflows/triggers are dynamic.
Decision: Use static scheduler, event router, generic executor, approval resume, worker callback, reflection, notification, usage, watchdog, and cleanup functions.
Consequences: User workflows stay data/compiled specs and runtime code stays testable.
Alternatives: Generate functions dynamically; put all work in one scheduler; build a custom queue first.

Title: Use internal EventContextPackets
Context: Workers, tools, apps, and workflows need to pass context without freeform worker chat or raw log forwarding.
Decision: Normalize app/workflow/task/worker outputs into internal EventContextPackets.
Consequences: Events become routeable, queryable, auditable, and billable while UI can update without waking main AI.
Alternatives: Freeform worker chat; raw logs to main AI; public ECP protocol from day one.

Title: Wake main AI only through reflection gates
Context: Waking main AI on every event recreates a high-token Manus-style orchestration loop.
Decision: Routine execution emits EventContextPackets and TaskReports; main AI wakes by default only for creation/user questions/edits/failures/rejections/cost/stuck/scheduled improvement.
Consequences: Recurring workflows stay cheaper and observable while main AI focuses on repair/explanation/improvement.
Alternatives: Main AI orchestrates every step; no reflection loop; user-only debugging.

Title: Use route-local Next 16 app structure
Context: The app has route groups but mixed ownership, global component buckets, broad client boundaries, and unclear app ownership.
Decision: Use a primary apps/app/src/app boundary, route groups, route-local _components/_actions/_hooks/_lib/_types, shared UI primitives, and server-first pages.
Consequences: Clarifies ownership and reduces client bundle risk before workflow UI work.
Alternatives: Keep current global buckets; global features folder only; copy prediction-market exactly.

Title: Use T3 Env as the env contract
Context: The repo needs typed validated env access, but the current app env aggregator can require unrelated integration secrets during builds.
Decision: Use T3 Env as the validation/type contract, Next/Vercel as app env loaders, @next/env only for standalone scripts, and scoped app env files.
Consequences: Keeps build validation and server/client safety while avoiding optional integration coupling.
Alternatives: Use process.env directly; use dotenv; use @next/env as validation; keep one huge app env aggregator.

Title: Deactivate legacy services from active workspace
Context: The old services tree was built to copy Manus-style decomposition and now conflicts with the workflow-first reset.
Decision: Remove services/* and packages/service-utils from the active workspace graph while keeping them temporarily as legacy reference.
Consequences: Active builds no longer include @jeriko service packages and backend can be redesigned around workflow contracts and adapters.
Alternatives: Keep fixing services; delete services immediately; move services under packages/backend.

Title: Deactivate redundant API app and legacy compose services
Context: apps/api and old service compose files still exposed inactive runtime boundaries after services were moved to legacy.
Decision: Move apps/api to legacy/deactivated-apps/api, move old service compose files to legacy/manus-clone/docker, and keep active Docker infrastructure-only.
Consequences: The active graph is smaller and API/server work stays in apps/app/app/api until a separate deploy boundary is justified.
Alternatives: Keep apps/api active; delete it immediately; keep old compose files in root.

Title: pnpm 11, Node 22.22.1, and strict linting runtime baseline
Context: Latest pnpm and lint-staged expose a real runtime floor: pnpm 11 requires Node >=22.13 and lint-staged 17 requires Node >=22.22.1.
Decision: Use pnpm 11.3.0 with Node 22.22.1+
Consequences: move pnpm policy to pnpm-workspace.yaml
Alternatives: enable strict engines
column9: Keeps package upgrades current and makes install-script trust explicit.
column10: Downgrade lint-staged; disable engineStrict; allow all build scripts; keep pnpm policy in .npmrc.

Title: Use docs.json as the single Mintlify docs config
Context: Latest Mintlify CLI generated docs.json from legacy mint.json and warned about legacy config while docs lint exposed stale starter links.
Decision: Use apps/docs/docs.json as the only Mintlify config; delete mint.json and update stale links/text.
Consequences: Removes duplicate config state and makes docs broken-link lint clean.
Alternatives: Keep both configs; keep only mint.json; delete docs app.

Title: Defer BaseHub fixes and evaluate Payload as the CMS replacement
Context: The current web CMS is BaseHub-backed and blocks root build, but the product direction no longer requires preserving BaseHub.
Decision: Do not fix BaseHub as the future CMS; isolate/remove the active BaseHub build dependency and evaluate Payload later after CMS boundaries are decided.
Consequences: Avoids wasting reset time on a CMS likely to be replaced while keeping build gates truthful.
Alternatives: Fix BaseHub now; delete web; install Payload immediately; ignore CMS build failures.

Title: Keep feature flags while lazy-loading product auth
Context: apps/web should keep feature flags, but module-level auth/database imports made web build require DATABASE_URL.
Decision: Keep feature flags and T3 Env; lazy-load product auth/analytics inside flag evaluation.
Consequences: Preserves feature flags while removing product DB coupling from marketing build.
Alternatives: Remove feature flags; use process.env; require DATABASE_URL for web builds.

Title: Adopt canonical engineering standards before further cleanup
Context: Cleanup and refactor work needs one mandatory rulebook to prevent package/env/Next.js drift.
Decision: Adopt docs/ai-workflow-os/00-ENGINEERING-STANDARDS.md as the read-first engineering standard.
Consequences: Reduces assumptions and makes future cleanup/refactor decisions reproducible.
Alternatives: Keep rules spread across docs/chat; rely only on generic instructions; add standards after cleanup.

Title: Require package-specific playbooks before critical refactors
Context: Repo-level standards are necessary but not enough for package-specific env/runtime/provider behavior.
Decision: Require playbooks before P0 package/app refactors and P1 architecture changes, using the package best-practices registry.
Consequences: Prevents package drift while avoiding exhaustive docs for every transitive dependency.
Alternatives: Document every dependency before continuing; rely only on repo-level standards; write playbooks after code changes.

Title: Build @repo/connectors around current Composio sessions
Context: The old Tool Router beta idea is now GA and implemented through Composio sessions; app connections/tools/triggers need a package boundary.
Decision: Create @repo/connectors with session-first Composio integration, provider-neutral contracts, mock/direct adapters, package-local env, and trigger/event normalization.
Consequences: Keeps Composio SDK/auth/session internals out of apps and lets @repo/ai/tools wrap side effects with platform policy.
Alternatives: Copy beta Tool Router API; put Composio directly in apps; expose raw connector tools to workflows.

Title: Policy-wrap connector actions in @repo/ai/tools
Context: AI SDK tools with execute run automatically and connector actions can produce external side effects.
Decision: Add a server-only @repo/ai/tools connector bridge with manifests, risk/permission metadata, approval policy, AI SDK conversion, and delegation to @repo/connectors.
Consequences: Prevents raw provider actions from being model-callable without platform policy while preserving Composio/direct connector isolation.
Alternatives: Expose raw Composio tools directly; put policy in @repo/connectors; require only app-local approval.

Title: Modernize @repo/ai by deleting the dead runtime layer
Context: The old AI package mixed AI SDK v6 dependencies with removed agent-service assumptions, E2B naming, custom stream/agent wrappers, local execution registries, and source-local tests.
Decision: Delete the dead runtime layer and use current AI SDK v6 primitives directly while keeping server-only platform tool policy under @repo/ai/tools.
Consequences: The package stops preserving fake runtime compatibility and can be validated as a real package boundary.
Alternatives: Keep compatibility exports; patch the local agent wrapper; delete all AI UI in the first runtime cleanup.

Title: Keep @repo/ai as a core AI SDK and platform-tool package
Context: After runtime cleanup, @repo/ai still carried old Manus workbench UI, canvas, chat components, hooks, providers, assistant-ui adapters, and browser/terminal/code panes with no active app consumers.
Decision: Reset @repo/ai to core AI SDK primitives, server helpers, provider/model helpers, platform tools, schema-only tool definitions, and connector bridge code; product AI UI starts in apps/app.
Consequences: Old @repo/ai component/hook/provider imports intentionally break and product UI must be rebuilt deliberately on AI SDK message parts and design-system primitives.
Alternatives: Keep salvage UI in the AI package; move old UI to design-system; keep assistant-ui as the main abstraction.

Title: Build custom AI UI on Vercel AI SDK
Context: The platform needs workflow-native uploads, downloads, files, voice-to-text, tool rendering, approvals, artifacts, sandbox views, and .flow editing.
Decision: Use Vercel AI SDK as the protocol/runtime layer and build app-local custom UI; use @ai-sdk/react in apps/app when chat UI is implemented and render from UIMessage.parts.
Consequences: The platform keeps full UI control but must implement and test composer/scrolling/uploads/tool cards/approvals/artifacts/voice UX.
Alternatives: Keep assistant-ui; adopt AI Elements wholesale; build package-level UI before app requirements are proven.

Title: Segment @repo/ai by AI SDK capability
Context: The cleaned AI package needs advanced AI SDK capabilities without becoming a UI dumping ground again.
Decision: Segment @repo/ai into agents, messages, server, media, models, retrieval, observability, testing, and server-only tools subpaths.
Consequences: Each feature has an intentional import path and React/assistant UI dependencies stay out of the core AI package.
Alternatives: One root barrel only; keep old lib/components/hooks/providers layout; split every feature into separate packages too early.

Title: .flow orchestrates AI SDK subagents tools and reporting
Context: The platform needs internal tools, connector tools, subagents, tool rendering, human approvals, abort/stop behavior, cron jobs, event triggers, and configurable subagent reporting.
Decision: Use .flow as orchestration policy, AI SDK as model/tool/agent primitive layer, and Inngest/runtime execution for durability/triggers/retries/waits/cancellation.
Consequences: Subagent reporting modes/tool permissions/cancellation policy become compiler-runtime concepts and UI renders normalized tool parts plus runtime events.
Alternatives: Let the main chat agent orchestrate everything; expose raw connector tools directly; model cancellation as only client stream abort.

Title: Use managed Inngest first behind a provider-neutral runtime boundary
Context: .flow needs durable execution for schedules, dynamic events, approvals, retries, waits, connector callbacks, subagent callbacks, cancellation, observability, and concurrency.
Decision: Use managed Inngest first for MVP workflow execution and keep durable execution behind a provider-neutral runtime adapter so @repo/flow does not import provider SDKs.
Consequences: We get durable execution primitives without operating runtime infrastructure while preserving self-hosted Inngest or Vercel Workflow as exit paths.
Alternatives: Self-host Inngest from day one; use Vercel Workflow as default now; build custom durable queue/runtime.

Title: Prefer Inngest over Vercel Workflow for dynamic .flow runtime
Context: The runtime needs dynamic user schedules, connector events, approvals, callbacks, fan-out, cancellation, concurrency, observability, and a provider-neutral .flow interpreter; Vercel Workflow is stronger for code-authored durable functions.
Decision: Use Inngest as the preferred MVP runtime for dynamic .flow execution and keep Vercel Workflow as a tracked evaluation path.
Consequences: Dynamic triggers stay DB rows handled by a small static scheduler/event-router/executor inventory and @repo/flow remains provider-neutral.
Alternatives: Use Vercel Workflow now; use both runtimes in MVP; self-host Inngest from day one; build custom durable runtime.

Title: Require durable runs and resumable UI reconnect
Context: The platform must continue active work when the browser refreshes, closes, disconnects, or returns later; current code has only partial resume hints.
Decision: Separate durable workflow execution from browser streams; reconnect UI by runId and event cursor; only explicit Stop/Cancel emits a durable cancellation event.
Consequences: Manus-style resume becomes a core runtime/API/UI requirement and route-local chat streams cannot be the sole source of truth.
Alternatives: Keep long-running work inside one app route stream; rely only on AI SDK resumable chat streams; treat browser close as cancellation.

Title: Harden Husky and lint-staged for large reset commits
Context: A failed commit attempt staged local pnpm store files and exposed a real Storybook React Hooks violation while lint-staged reverted the worktree.
Decision: Keep current Husky/lint-staged, use a minimal local-only pre-commit hook, explicit ACMR filtering, serial execution, relative paths, bounded arg length, .pnpm-store ignore, and repo-aware chunking/filtering.
Consequences: Large reset commits become more deterministic and generated local store files cannot enter the index while real active-code lint failures still block commits.
Alternatives: Bypass hooks; disable lint-staged stash/revert; run full repo lint in pre-commit; replace local tooling during the commit fix.
